title: Running PHP from the Command Line
keywords: running php from the command line
learning_outcomes: Explain what running php from the command line contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: checking the php version.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: PHP source is parsed and executed by the PHP runtime. Tags mark PHP regions, statements and blocks define the program structure, and CLI and web-server execution have different inputs and output contexts. In this lesson, focus on checking the php version; then compare it with executing scripts. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use running php from the command line when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: PHP source is parsed and executed by the PHP runtime. Tags mark PHP regions, statements and blocks define the program structure, and CLI and web-server execution have different inputs and output contexts. For running php from the command line, begin with checking the php version. Also distinguish executing scripts; passing arguments to scripts; reading command-line arguments. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
